title: At the Agency: The Sword Bearer Crisis, 1887
description: You are an interpreter at the Crow Agency. Over three tense moments, you must help others speak, decide what to report, and judge whom to trust as conflict grows from a raid to a military clash and then to a political reckoning.
learningObjectives: Describe what happened at the Crow Agency during the Sword Bearer incident of 1887.
Explain the positions of Crow leaders, the agent, and the army.
Evaluate how the incident was reported by the people involved.

player.name: The Interpreter
player.brief: You translate between Crow speakers and U.S. officials. Your words can calm, sharpen, or redirect a crisis.

sharedContext.text: In fall 1887, a party of young Crow men returned from a raid on the Piegans with captured horses. Agent Henry Williamson called for troops after gunfire at the agency, and tensions rose until fighting broke out on November 5. Later, Crow leaders met the agent in council and asked for the return of prisoners. Your task is to navigate these moments as an interpreter, comparing what happened with how each side described it.

spans.quote: In fall 1887 a group of young Crow Indians led by a Messianic figure
stealing some sixty horses.
Agent H. E. Williamson called for troops to be sent from nearby Fort Custer.
Finally, the situation came to head on November 5.
I want the Great Father to let the Page 2 eight Crow prisoners now held at Fort Snelling, come home to us pretty quick

assumptions.text: The player character is an agency interpreter present in all three stages.
assumptions.rationale: The teacher brief assigns the student this role, but the source documents do not name such a person in these scenes.

assumptions.text: Each stage uses a small set of rooms at or near the Crow Agency to structure movement and conversation.
assumptions.rationale: The documents describe events and meetings, not exact playable layouts.

assumptions.text: Private motives and knowledge limits are inferred from each person's actions and statements.
assumptions.rationale: The sources record public words and actions, not inner thoughts.

assumptions.text: A Crow leader can be met near the agency during the October alarm to voice concern before wider fighting.
assumptions.rationale: The October letter does not name a Crow speaker in that moment, but the simulation needs a Crow interlocutor.

assumptions.text: A brief playable parley is staged around the failed peace effort before or during the November 5 crisis.
assumptions.rationale: The background mentions a failed meeting with Crow leaders, but gives no transcript.

assumptions.text: In the December council, the interpreter can choose how strongly to press the prisoners' issue or let the discussion shift.
assumptions.rationale: The source gives minutes, not the player's intervention.

assumptions.text: Landmarks such as a telegraph desk, council stove, and prisoner photograph display are added to make sources inspectable.
assumptions.rationale: These props are plausible teaching devices, not documented scene fixtures.

summary.text: Williamson presents the raiders as a direct threat to the agency. He reports gunfire, says police could not act, praises Dudley's prompt response, and asks Washington for authority to arrest the raiders and other defiant Indians at once.

spans.quote: firing their guns into buildings in defiant and threatening manner
my police were unable to do so
I deem the arrest of these raiders and other defiant Indians at once as absolutely necessary

summary.text: Plenty Coos asks for practical help: finish surveying Crow land and bring the prisoners home so they can support their families and work. His words show concern for labor, land, and the treatment of Crow men after the fighting.

spans.quote: I want you to tell the Great Father to send him here next year to finish surveying our land
eight Crow prisoners now held at Fort Snelling, come home to us pretty quick
can take care of their cattle

summary.text: Dudley represents military force at the agency. Williamson reports that Dudley sent companies quickly, sought further instructions, and worked under limits to protect the agency and its employees.

spans.quote: I called on Genl [General] Dudley commanding Fort Custer for troops to arrest them.
Gen’l Dudley has been prompt in his action and is telegraphing Department Headquarters for full instructions.
The Officer in command having instructions to protect Agency and Employees only.

summary.text: Big Shoulder Blade supports Mr. Cummins and also frames Sword Bearer as a single foolish man who is now dead. He praises Williamson's treatment of the Crow while still asking that the prisoners be returned quickly.

spans.quote: We all like Mr. Cummins as one of our own people.
he is gone (dead) now.
It will be good for you to get the eight Crow prisoners back as soon as you can

stages.title: October 1: The Alarm at the Agency

sharedContext.text: A raiding party has returned with captured horses. Williamson says six men rode around the agency firing into buildings. Troops from Fort Custer have arrived, but the officer says his orders are limited. As interpreter, you must decide whether to push for immediate arrests or for a calmer approach before the crisis widens.

spans.quote: A party of twenty Crows with captured horses returned five o’clock yesterday evening
Six of them road [rode] around Agency firing their guns into buildings
Three companies arrived at Ten O’clock.
The Officer in command having instructions to protect Agency and Employees only.

publicPosition.text: Williamson insists that the raiders have threatened the agency and must be arrested at once. He wants the War Department's backing because agency police could not carry out the arrests alone.

spans.quote: The raiders defied police and military.
my police were unable to do so
ask that orders be so issued by the War Department

privateContext.persona: A pressured administrator trying to prove control in a public emergency.
privateContext.motivations: Restore order fast, protect employees, and show superiors that he acted decisively.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: He wants the written record to justify calling in troops before anyone in Washington blames him for losing control.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows what he has seen at the agency and what soldiers have reported to him, but not how every Crow leader reads the crisis.

spans.quote: I called on Genl [General] Dudley commanding Fort Custer for troops to arrest them.
I deem the arrest of these raiders and other defiant Indians at once as absolutely necessary

publicPosition.text: Dudley has responded quickly, but his command is operating under instructions to protect the agency and employees. He is waiting for fuller authority while preparing for force if needed.

spans.quote: Three companies arrived at Ten O’clock.
The Officer in command having instructions to protect Agency and Employees only.
telegraphing Department Headquarters for full instructions

privateContext.persona: A professional officer wary of acting beyond orders in a politically charged scene.
privateContext.motivations: Maintain discipline, avoid blame for inaction, and keep his command's role formally legitimate.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: He prefers clearer authority before a wider operation, even if civilians press him to move faster.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows troop positions and his orders, but not the deeper local relationships inside Crow politics.

spans.quote: The Officer in command having instructions to protect Agency and Employees only.
Gen’l Dudley has been prompt in his action

publicPosition.text: A respected Crow leader warns that broad arrests could turn a raid into a larger break with the agency. He wants the interpreter to carry words carefully before soldiers act.

privateContext.persona: A pragmatic leader trying to shield his people from a wider military response.
privateContext.motivations: Separate the raiders from the rest of the Crow and prevent panic from becoming collective punishment.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: He wants space for later negotiation and fears that official reports will flatten Crow divisions into one hostile camp.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows local opinion better than the soldiers do, but cannot control armed young men already acting defiantly.

spans.quote: some of the band of horse thieves to start firing their guns into various buildings at the Agency.

content.text: The draft frames the situation as an attack on the agency and stresses that arrests are urgently necessary. It is already written in the language of official justification.

spans.quote: firing their guns into buildings in defiant and threatening manner without provocation.

content.text: The note shows that the troops' mission is narrower than Williamson wants. The army is present, but its authority is not unlimited.

decision.title: How will you frame the crisis?
decision.prompt: Williamson is ready to send his account upward and press for arrests. Soldiers are present but constrained. Do you reinforce the demand for immediate force, or stress caution and distinction between raiders and the wider Crow community?

options.label: Urge Williamson to open a channel with Crow leaders before wider arrests.
Support Williamson's demand for immediate arrests and stronger military backing.
Translate narrowly and avoid shaping either side's position.

sharedContext.text: By early November, tensions have not eased. The background account says a peace meeting with Crow leaders failed, and fighting broke out between Companies E and K of the 1st Cavalry and about 150 Crows. Sword Bearer was killed, and prisoners were later taken. In this stage, you face the problem of how that confrontation is translated and remembered while it is still unfolding.

spans.quote: After a meeting between General Thomas H. Ruger and several Crow leaders not involved with Sword Bearer’s group failed to achieve peace
a fight broke out between Companies E and K of the 1st Cavalry and about 150 Crows.
In the end the Crows retreated, and Sword Bearer was killed.
Eventually, eight Crows (considered to be ringleaders) were taken prisoner

privateContext.hiddenInterests: He wants the military role remembered as necessary, not reckless.

decision.title: What story will your translation support?
decision.prompt: The crisis has turned into open violence. You can help frame it as a necessary military response, or preserve distinctions between Sword Bearer's band and other Crow leaders for what comes next. Which line do you carry forward?

options.label: Record the clash carefully and preserve room for a later council.
Translate the event as proof that a broad hard line is justified.
Emphasize that some Crow leaders were not part of Sword Bearer's band.

sharedContext.text: Weeks after the fight, Crow leaders meet the agent in council. Plenty Coos asks for land surveying to continue and for the prisoners at Fort Snelling to return home. Williamson then shifts the discussion to whether Mr. Cummins and his family should be adopted into the tribe. As interpreter, you must decide whether to keep attention on the prisoners or let the meeting follow the agent's turn.

spans.quote: I want the Great Father to let the Page 2 eight Crow prisoners now held at Fort Snelling, come home to us pretty quick
We don’t think that they have done anything very bad.
Agent I have been told that some of you desire to adopt Mr. Cummins
there was no objection made by any of the Indians present, their consent was unanimous.

publicPosition.text: Plenty Coos asks the government to continue surveying Crow land and to send the prisoners home quickly so they can work and care for their families and cattle. He does not present them as men who have done great wrong.

spans.quote: finish surveying our land and to show us what is to be done
come home to us pretty quick
We don’t think that they have done anything very bad.

privateContext.persona: A measured leader using practical needs to press a political demand.
privateContext.motivations: Get men back home, reduce the damage of imprisonment, and keep the discussion on Crow interests rather than agency priorities.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: He knows that labor, cattle, and land policy make a stronger argument to officials than grief alone.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows the community's needs, but not what federal offices will decide about prisoners held far away.

spans.quote: come home to us pretty quick

publicPosition.text: When Plenty Coos raises the prisoners, Williamson turns to another issue: whether Mr. Cummins and his family should be adopted into the tribe. He keeps the meeting orderly by moving to a question that can end in a formal consensus.

spans.quote: Agent I have been told that some of you desire to adopt Mr. Cummins
their consent was unanimous.

privateContext.persona: An experienced official steering a delicate meeting toward safer ground.
privateContext.motivations: Control the council's agenda, secure a clear result, and avoid dwelling on the prisoners where he may have less room to promise anything.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: Changing the subject lets him record harmony on adoption rather than pressure on the prisoner question.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows the council procedure and what he can put in writing, but not how long Crow frustration over the prisoners will last.

spans.quote: Agent I have been told that some of you desire to adopt Mr. Cummins
I certify on honor that the above is a true report

publicPosition.text: Big Shoulder Blade supports the adoption of Mr. Cummins and his family, praises Williamson's treatment of the Crow, but also wants the prisoners back quickly so they can work. He presents Sword Bearer as one foolish man, now dead.

get the eight Crow prisoners back as soon as you can

privateContext.persona: A careful speaker balancing respect, criticism, and practical demands.
privateContext.motivations: Keep relations workable with the agent while still arguing for the prisoners' return.
privateContext.hiddenInterests: By praising Williamson, he may hope to make the request harder to dismiss.
privateContext.knowledgeHorizon: He knows the council mood and the value of respectful speech, but not how Washington will weigh the request.

spans.quote: You (to Agent Williamson) have always treated us well.
It will be good for you to get the eight Crow prisoners back as soon as you can

decision.title: What will this council be remembered for?
decision.prompt: The council can become a formal record about adoption, or a stronger appeal about the prisoners and the meaning of the recent violence. As interpreter, do you press the prisoner issue, accept Williamson's redirection, or keep both topics in view?

options.label: Help the Crow speakers keep the prisoners at the center of the appeal.
Balance both topics and record the council as a mixed petition.

endings.title: Early Ending: Force Before Dialogue
endings.summary: You back Williamson's demand for immediate arrests and stronger military authority. The agency record hardens early around danger and control. You leave little room to separate the raiders from the wider Crow community, and your role as interpreter becomes part of the machinery of escalation.

historicalOutcome.text: The sources show that Williamson did ask for immediate arrests, stating that the raiders had defied police and military, and that he considered arresting them "absolutely necessary." Fighting later broke out on November 5, Sword Bearer was killed, and eight Crow prisoners were eventually taken.

spans.quote: I deem the arrest of these raiders and other defiant Indians at once as absolutely necessary
Finally, the situation came to head on November 5.
Eventually, eight Crows (considered to be ringleaders) were taken prisoner

endings.divergence: This ending compresses events by making the player's support for immediate force end the playable story before the later council documented in the sources.
reflectionQuestions: How does Williamson's letter justify urgent force?
What is lost when later Crow voices are not heard?
Does official language make escalation seem inevitable?

endings.title: Ending: The Army's Version Wins
endings.summary: You help fix the November clash as a straightforward military necessity. The later distinctions between different Crow leaders fade from view. The crisis becomes a story of suppression, not argument, and the prisoner's names remain more visible than their own explanations.

historicalOutcome.text: The sources state that a peace effort failed, fighting broke out between Companies E and K and about 150 Crows, Sword Bearer was killed, and eight prisoners were taken after the fight. A later council did occur, where Crow leaders asked for those prisoners to return.

spans.quote: failed to achieve peace, a fight broke out between Companies E and K of the 1st Cavalry and about 150 Crows.
In the end the Crows retreated, and Sword Bearer was killed.
eight Crow prisoners now held at Fort Snelling, come home to us pretty quick

endings.divergence: This ending stops before the documented December council, so it underrepresents the later Crow effort to shape the record and ask for the prisoners' return.
reflectionQuestions: Why might military reports flatten political differences on the Crow side?
How do prisoner lists and casualty outcomes shape memory?
What changes when later council testimony is ignored?

endings.title: Ending: A Sharper Appeal for Return
endings.summary: You keep the prisoners at the center of the council. The meeting becomes a stronger moral and practical appeal about families, work, and whether the accused men had done "anything very bad." This does not erase the fight, but it changes what the council is made to mean.

historicalOutcome.text: In the historical record, Plenty Coos did ask that the prisoners at Fort Snelling come home quickly so they could help their families work and care for cattle. The prisoners were not immediately returned; the background note says they were held at Fort Snelling until spring 1888, and most were then sent to Carlisle.

spans.quote: come home to us pretty quick
were held at Fort Snelling until spring 1888
All of the remaining prisoners, except for Deaf Bull, were transferred to the Carlisle Industrial School

endings.divergence: This ending imagines the interpreter making the prisoner issue more dominant in the council record than the surviving minutes show.
reflectionQuestions: Why does Plenty Coos frame the prisoners' return as a labor and family issue?
What does this tell us about how Crow leaders argued with federal officials?
How might the written minutes have looked different if this emphasis had prevailed?

endings.title: Ending: The Council as It Survives in the Record
endings.summary: You preserve a mixed record: Crow leaders ask for prisoners to return, but Williamson turns to the adoption of Mr. Cummins and his family, where unanimous agreement is easy to certify. The result is not silence, but a redirection. The written source itself becomes part of the lesson.

historicalOutcome.text: This ending matches the surviving minutes most closely. Plenty Coos requested the return of the eight prisoners, saying they had not done anything very bad. Williamson then asked about adopting Mr. Cummins and his family, and the minutes record unanimous consent. In the broader outcome, the prisoners remained away for months and some were later sent to Carlisle.

spans.quote: We don’t think that they have done anything very bad.
Agent I have been told that some of you desire to adopt Mr. Cummins
their consent was unanimous.
were held at Fort Snelling until spring 1888

endings.divergence: This ending is the closest match to the documented record.
reflectionQuestions: Why might Williamson shift from prisoners to adoption?
What can official minutes reveal, and what can they hide?
Whose priorities dominate the surviving record of the council?
